_note: Interactive multiple-choice bank. Keys match section ids in build.py. 'answer' is the 0-based index of the correct option. 'why' is shown after answering. Edit here, then run: cd docs && python3 build.py

module-01.title: Warm-up: how much do you already know?

questions.q: Choose the correct verb: The team ___ been training every morning since Monday.
questions.why: 'The team' is a collective noun and takes a singular verb in British usage: The team has been training.

questions.q: Which is correct? Neither of the boys ___ late for practice.
questions.why: 'Neither' is singular, so it takes 'was'.

questions.q: He ran ___ down the steps.
questions.why: 'Quickly' is an adverb and describes how he ran.

questions.q: If I ___ taller, I would play centre.
questions.why: In an imaginary 'if' clause, English uses 'were': If I were taller…

questions.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
questions.why: The question mark sits inside the speech marks, and 'shouted Mum' continues the sentence so 'shouted' stays lowercase.

questions.q: Which sentence keeps its tense consistent?
options: He walks into the room and saw the trophy.
He walked into the room and saw the trophy.
He walked into the room and sees the trophy.
questions.why: Both verbs stay in the past: walked … saw.

questions.q: Yesterday we ___ to the beach.
questions.why: 'Yesterday' is finished time, so use the past simple: went.

questions.q: He ___ his homework an hour ago.
questions.why: 'An hour ago' is a finished time, so 'finished' — not the present perfect.

questions.q: The list of names ___ long.
questions.why: The subject is 'list', not 'names': the list was long.

questions.q: There ___ three reasons for this.
questions.why: The real subject is 'three reasons' (plural), so 'are'.

questions.q: The news ___ good.
questions.why: 'News' looks plural but is singular: the news is good.

questions.q: Which is punctuated correctly?
questions.why: A comma sits inside the speech marks, and the reporting clause 'he said' is separated by commas on both sides.

questions.q: Which sentence is a complex sentence?
options: It rained and we played on.
Although it was raining, we played on.
questions.why: A complex sentence has a main clause plus a subordinate clause introduced by 'although'.

questions.q: Which sentence is in a different tense from the others?
options: She opened the door, looked around and screamed.
questions.why: The first two are past simple; 'has finished' is present perfect.

questions.q: Which uses apostrophes correctly?
options: It's raining, and the city's trams are slow.
Its raining, and the city's trams are slow.
It's raining, and the citys trams are slow.
questions.why: 'It's' = it is; 'city's' shows possession.

questions.q: Which is the best replacement for 'very nice' describing food?
questions.why: 'Delicious' is precise and describes taste; 'big' and 'fine' are vague.

questions.q: Which is the best replacement for 'very tired'?
questions.why: 'Exhausted' already means very tired, so it replaces the whole phrase.

questions.q: Which sentence contains a simile?
options: Her laugh was like a door slamming.
The wind clawed at the windows.
questions.why: A simile compares using 'like' or 'as'.

questions.q: Which sentence uses personification?
options: The wind clawed at the windows.
Her laugh was like a door slamming.
questions.why: The wind is given a human action — clawing.

questions.q: Which sentence shows embarrassment rather than telling it?
options: A red flush crept up his neck; he studied his shoes as if they held the answers.
questions.why: Showing gives the reader evidence (a flush, a gesture) and lets them name the feeling.

questions.q: Which phrase is a cliché you should avoid?
questions.why: Examiners have read it thousands of times — clichés score nothing.

questions.q: Which verb best describes heavy, slow walking?
questions.why: 'Trudged' means slow, heavy walking — the others are fast or light.

questions.q: Which weak-to-strong pairing is mismatched?
questions.why: Freezing means very cold, not very hot — that pair is wrong.

questions.q: What happens at midnight on the island?
options: A whistle blows and climbers race up a tower of buns.
The buns are blessed and eaten.
The ferry brings the crowds over.
questions.why: This is an R1 question — the answer is stated plainly in the text.

questions.q: Who are the climbers?
questions.why: The text says they are students, or chefs, or delivery riders — ordinary people.

questions.q: Why was the race stopped in 1978?
options: the tower collapsed and forty people were hurt
questions.why: The tower collapsed in a heap of bamboo and forty people were hurt.

questions.q: 'An island that knows every one of their names' suggests the community is…
questions.why: Knowing everyone's name shows a small, tight community.

questions.q: The writer says the race came back 'even better' because…
options: the risk is now shared and understood rather than hidden
questions.why: The text says not because danger is gone, but because the risk is now shared.

questions.q: Which of these is an implicit (R2) question?
options: Where does the race take place?
How many people were hurt in 1978?
What impression does the writer give of the climbers?
questions.why: R2 questions ask about attitude and impression, not facts you can point to.

questions.q: In a summary, you should…
questions.why: Copied phrases do not count for R5 — paraphrase everything.

questions.q: How many points should you select?
options: as many as you can find
only those relevant to the stated focus
only the first and last paragraph
questions.why: Read the focus line twice; every point must serve it.

questions.q: Which is NOT allowed in a summary?
questions.why: A summary has no opinion — ever.

questions.q: Which connective best links an opposite idea?
questions.why: 'However' signals contrast; the others add ideas.

questions.q: What happens if you go over the word limit?
options: nothing, as long as it is good
you get extra marks for detail
questions.why: Stay at or under the limit — going over costs marks.

questions.q: You are writing to your headteacher. Which opening is right?
questions.why: Formal register, with a proper salutation.

questions.q: Which sign-off matches 'Dear Sir/Madam'?
questions.why: 'Sir/Madam' means you do not know the name, so: Yours faithfully.

questions.q: Which opener is informal register?
options: I am writing to complain about the service.
questions.why: Contractions and a chatty tone belong in a message to a friend.

questions.q: In an article, how do you involve the reader?
options: by using first and second person and rhetorical questions
by writing only in the third person
questions.why: 'Ever noticed how…? You probably have.' pulls the reader in.

questions.q: Which text type uses sub-headings like Introduction, Findings, Recommendations?
questions.why: A report is factual and formally structured.

questions.q: You miss one of the three bullet points in a directed writing task. The result is…
options: extra credit for the other two
questions.why: A missing bullet caps the mark — check every cue before you finish.

questions.q: Before any extended writing you should…
questions.why: A five-line plan is worth two marks of structure.

questions.q: Descriptive writing should be built around…
questions.why: Decide one feeling the place should leave, and choose details that serve it.

questions.q: Which technique controls the pace of a narrative?
questions.why: Short sentences speed up; long sentences slow down.

questions.q: Which ending should you avoid?
questions.why: 'It was all a dream' endings feel cheap and earn nothing.

questions.q: You show a character is brave by…
options: showing an action: he stepped between his sister and the dog
questions.why: Show character through action, not by labelling them.

questions.q: You write only: 'The writer uses a metaphor here.' How many marks does naming the device earn?
options: none — you must explain the effect
questions.why: Naming earns nothing. Explain what it makes the reader see, feel or think.

questions.q: Q-E-E stands for…
questions.why: Quote the words, Explain the technique, then state the Effect on the reader.

questions.q: 'The old tram rattles up the hill.' What does 'rattles' suggest?
questions.why: A rattle suggests something old and worn.

questions.q: Which is the better analysis?
options: The writer personifies the tram, which makes the climb feel unhurried and timeless.
questions.why: The second explains the effect on the reader — that is where the marks are.

questions.q: 'came back small, careful, and wrapped in safety nets.' The three-part list creates…
questions.why: The list slows the sentence and feels measured and controlled.

questions.q: Every effects answer must include…
questions.why: Quote the exact words, then explain — evidence first.
